title: The tapestry that tells of conquest
text: The Bayeux Tapestry {{1}} made in the 1070s, most likely in southern England, and strictly speaking it {{2}} not a tapestry at all but an embroidery, stitched rather than woven. A seventy-metre strip of linen, {{3}} tells the story of the Norman conquest in vivid coloured wool, it carries us from oath-taking in France to a corpse-strewn hillside in Sussex. William of Normandy, {{4}} claimed the English crown, appears throughout, ever watchful. {{5}} well as a chronicle of events, the work is unmistakable propaganda, justifying the conquest for those who might question it. {{6}} margins, crowded with lions, ships and farming scenes, are a treasure trove of everyday medieval life. The Battle of Hastings, {{7}} the English king Harold is struck down, fills the final scenes, and the cloth has {{8}} displayed in the Norman town of Bayeux since at least 1476.

gaps.explanation: 'Where' refers back to the battle as the scene.
